ai.definition: Flow batteries are electrochemical storage systems that store energy in liquid electrolytes contained within external tanks. The energy can be scaled independently by adjusting the volume of the electrolyte tanks, which allows for long-duration storage.
ai.howItWorks: In a flow battery, two tanks hold different electrolyte solutions. These solutions pass through an electrochemical cell stack where they react to store and release energy. Power output is controlled by the size of the cell stack, while energy capacity is determined by the volume of electrolyte in the tanks.
ai.problemSolved: Flow batteries address the need for long-duration storage that can support grid-scale applications without the limitations on energy density found in solid-state battery technologies.
ai.manufacturing: Manufacturing involves creating the electrochemical cell stacks, designing and constructing the liquid electrolyte storage tanks, and integrating these components into a functional system. The process requires precision in material selection and assembly to ensure efficient operation and long lifetimes.
ai.buildProcess: The build process includes component design, fabrication of cell stacks using materials like electrodes and membranes, tank construction, and integration testing to ensure the system operates as intended before deployment.
ai.costDrivers: Cost drivers include electrode and membrane material costs, electrolyte formulation, tank manufacturing, and system integration. The scalability of flow batteries can reduce per-unit cost for large-scale projects but may increase initial setup costs due to larger component sizes.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: flow batteries are expected to see increased deployment in grid storage applications as demand for long-duration energy storage solutions grows, particularly with the rise of renewable energy sources that require stable energy supply over extended periods.
ai.regulation: Regulations vary by region but generally focus on safety standards for handling hazardous chemicals and environmental impact assessments. There is ongoing development of specific guidelines for flow battery systems to ensure they meet regulatory requirements without hindering innovation.
ai.risks: Safety risks are primarily related to the use of potentially flammable electrolytes, which require careful design and operational protocols. Environmental concerns include disposal of spent electrolytes and potential leaching of materials into the environment if not properly managed.
ai.profitability: Profitability is variable and depends on market demand for long-duration storage solutions, regulatory support, and cost reductions through technology improvements and economies of scale in production.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future developments may include advancements in electrolyte chemistry to improve energy density and reduce costs, as well as innovations in cell stack design to enhance efficiency and durability. Integration with renewable energy systems is expected to drive further adoption.

glossary.def: A type of electrochemical battery that stores energy in liquid electrolyte tanks, allowing for independent scaling of power and energy capacity.
The fluid component of a flow battery that contains the ions used to store and release electrical charge through chemical reactions.
A series of electrochemical cells connected in series or parallel to form a larger power output unit within a flow battery system.

subsystems.name: Electrolyte and tanks
subsystems.role: stores the energy as two liquids in separate tanks; doubling the tank volume doubles the stored energy without touching the stack.
parts: vanadium, iron, zinc or organic redox salts dissolved in acid or alkaline solution

subsystems.name: Cell stack
subsystems.role: converts electrical energy to chemical energy and back; more cells or larger cells mean more power.

subsystems.name: Hydraulic loop
subsystems.role: pumps both electrolytes through the stacks at a steady rate.

subsystems.name: Power conversion
subsystems.role: turns the stack's direct current into grid-compatible alternating current in both directions.

subsystems.name: Thermal and rebalancing system
subsystems.role: keeps electrolyte in its working temperature range and corrects the slow migration of active material across the membrane.
parts: rebalancing cell or electrolyte re-mixing loop

subsystems.name: Controls
subsystems.role: runs charge and discharge cycles, tracks state of charge and protects the stack.
parts: SCADA link to the grid operator

buildSteps.title: Produce the active material
buildSteps.detail: Vanadium pentoxide is reduced and dissolved in sulfuric acid to make electrolyte at roughly 1.5–2 moles of vanadium per litre — often sourced from steel-slag or mining residues. Iron, zinc and organic flow chemistries start from cheaper salts or synthesised molecules.

buildSteps.title: Cast the membrane
buildSteps.detail: A perfluorosulfonic-acid polymer or a hydrocarbon alternative is cast into a thin film a few tens of micrometres thick. It must let charge-carrying ions through while blocking the active species from mixing.

buildSteps.title: Make the electrodes and plates
buildSteps.detail: Carbon felt or cloth is heat-treated, and conductive carbon-polymer composite plates are moulded with flow channels that spread electrolyte evenly across the felt.

buildSteps.title: Stack the cells
buildSteps.detail: Electrode, membrane and plate are repeated tens to over a hundred times, compressed between end plates so each cell sits at about 1.2–1.6 V and the stack totals tens to hundreds of volts.

buildSteps.title: Build the hydraulic loop
buildSteps.detail: Tanks, pumps, pipework and sensors are assembled, usually inside shipping-container-sized modules that can be trucked to site and bolted together.

buildSteps.title: Fill and condition
buildSteps.detail: Both tanks are filled with electrolyte and the stack is cycled gently so the electrodes and membrane reach stable performance.

buildSteps.title: Connect and commission
buildSteps.detail: The inverter is tied to the grid transformer, and charge/discharge cycles are run to verify round-trip efficiency, typically 65–80% for vanadium systems, and to calibrate state of charge.

buildSteps.title: Operate and service
buildSteps.detail: The system runs for 20 years or more with tens of thousands of cycles; maintenance is mostly pump, sensor and electrolyte top-up work rather than cell replacement.

prerequisites.why: the cell only works if one ion can cross while the two electrolytes stay separate; membrane cost is a large share of system cost.

prerequisites.tech: Vanadium and other redox-active salts at scale
prerequisites.why: electrolyte is the single biggest cost item, so supply of vanadium, iron or cheap organic molecules sets the economics.
the stack produces DC and the grid needs AC in both directions.
they could undercut vanadium, but most are only in pilot or early commercial use.

prerequisites.tech: Very low-cost tank and piping manufacturing
prerequisites.why: long duration is won by buying cheap liquid containment, not expensive electrochemistry.

pathway.milestone: vanadium systems of tens to hundreds of megawatts connected to grids, including a 100 MW / 400 MWh installation in Dalian, China, energised in 2022
pathway.unlocks: multi-hour storage that can be cycled daily for decades without capacity fade.

pathway.milestone: iron, zinc and organic flow chemistries moving from pilots to commercial production
pathway.unlocks: storage that does not depend on vanadium prices and can be built from abundant materials.

pathway.milestone: electrolyte leasing and reuse, with the liquid recovered and refurbished at end of life
pathway.unlocks: much lower lifetime cost, since the electrolyte outlives the stack.

pathway.milestone: routines of 12–100 hour storage built alongside wind and solar farms
pathway.unlocks: firm power through multi-day calm or cloudy periods, displacing gas peaking plants.
